input:
## Start-up

Prior to the protected equipment being pressurised, it is important to ensure that the relief valve is fully ready to perform its protective function. Firstly, the nameplate should be read and the set pressure verified against the equipment data sheet, since a valve with an incorrect set pressure will not provide protection at the intended limit. A thorough inspection of the valve body, the inlet line, and the discharge line should also be carried out for damage, debris, or accumulated liquid. It should furthermore be confirmed that the inlet block valve and the outlet block valve are completely open, and both valves should be secured in the open position by means of the fitted seal or lock. The discharge line should be checked to ensure that it runs freely and openly to its destination, and all drain points on the discharge side should be closed. The bonnet drain and any tell-tale tapping should likewise be checked for clarity. The pressure in the protected equipment should then be raised gradually whilst the gauge is closely observed. As the pressure approaches the normal operating level, the operator should listen carefully at the valve, as the valve must remain firmly shut and silent below its set pressure. All flanges on the inlet and discharge lines should be inspected for leakage whilst the pressure is held. In the event that the valve simmers, chatters, or leaks at normal operating pressure, the start-up should be stopped, the equipment depressurised, and the valve reported for bench testing. In this way, the start-up is completed with the valve in service, its isolation proved open, and the discharge route clear.

## Normal operation

Throughout the period in which the protected equipment remains pressurised, it is essential that the relief valve is kept continuously available. The line should be walked on each round and the valve proved as found. Operators should confirm that the inlet and outlet block valves remain fully open and secured, bearing in mind that a closed block valve silently removes the protection without any indication at the equipment itself. Careful attention should be paid to any passing at the valve seat, and the discharge line should be felt for warmth that cannot be explained by steady operation. After any lift, the discharge outlet should be examined for frost or condensate, and any obstruction at the outlet should be cleared before it has the opportunity to freeze or plug. The area around the valve should be kept clear so that access can be gained at short notice. It must be emphasised that the valve should never be gagged, its outlet should never be plugged, and its inlet should never be blanked in order to stop a leak; similarly, the set pressure should never be adjusted at the line, as set-pressure adjustment is a workshop activity that is carried out on the bench following removal. Any simmering, leakage, or lift should be recorded in the shift log together with the equipment pressure at the time, and a valve that lifts, leaks, or fails to reseat should be reported to the shift supervisor within the same shift. Normal operation therefore places few demands on the valve itself, and the round serves to demonstrate that nothing has compromised its protection.

## Alarms

Two alarms are recognised in this chapter. Any other alarm arising on the protected equipment should be handled in accordance with the equipment chapter, and the relief valve should be left as found unless one of the actions described below states otherwise.

High pressure in the protected equipment. The operator should proceed to the relief valve and confirm that the valve is discharging, which will be evidenced by the discharge line warming and by the valve being audible at the outlet. The equipment pressure should be watched whilst the valve is discharging. If the pressure is seen to fall, the equipment should be held steady and the valve allowed to reseat. However, if the pressure continues to rise even though the valve is discharging, the source of pressure to the equipment should be shut off: the feed should be stopped, the heating input should be stopped, and the shift supervisor should be informed immediately. The operator should remain at the equipment until the pressure is falling and the report has been taken by the supervisor.

Relief valve passing. In this condition, the discharge line remains warm, or flow can be heard at the valve, even after the equipment pressure has returned to its normal level. The shift supervisor should be informed and the equipment pressure kept under close observation. A maintenance request should be raised for the removal and bench testing of the valve. It is important to note that the valve should not be isolated whilst the equipment remains pressurised, as the equipment retains its protection until a planned changeover or shutdown can be arranged. Each alarm, together with the action that was taken in response to it, should be recorded in the shift log before the shift comes to an end. The two responses are therefore quite distinct in nature: the first demonstrates that the valve is working when the pressure is high, whilst the second reports the valve when it passes at normal pressure.

## Shutdown

The relief valve should only be taken out of service once the protected equipment has been fully depressurised. The equipment pressure should be reduced to zero by means of the normal let-down route and the resulting state proved at the gauge. The vent on the protected equipment should be opened and it should be proved that no pressure remains prior to any line being broken. The inlet and outlet block valves should then be closed and the isolation lock and tag applied. The discharge line should be drained to its drain point, and the drain should be left open for the duration of the period in which the valve is out of service. The valve should be handed over for removal only when the isolation has been proved and duly recorded, as removal, overhaul, and bench testing fall under the maintenance procedure. When the valve is returned from the bench, it should be restored in accordance with the start-up section: the nameplate should be checked against the test certificate, the block valves proved open and secured, and the first pressurisation carefully watched. Shutdown thus leaves the equipment depressurised, the valve isolated and drained, and its return governed by the checks set out at start-up.

## Start-up

Before the protected equipment is pressurised, prove the relief valve ready for service. Read the nameplate and check the set pressure against the equipment data sheet; a valve with the wrong set pressure gives no protection at the intended limit. Inspect the valve body, the inlet line, and the discharge line for damage, debris, and standing liquid. Confirm that the inlet block valve and the outlet block valve are fully open, and secure both valves in the open position with the fitted seal or lock. Confirm that the discharge line runs open to its destination and that every drain point on the discharge side is closed. Check that the bonnet drain and any tell-tale tapping are clear. Raise the pressure in the protected equipment slowly and watch the gauge as the pressure climbs. Listen at the valve as the pressure approaches the normal operating level: the valve must stay shut and silent below its set pressure. Inspect every flange on the inlet and discharge lines for leakage while the pressure is held. If the valve simmers, chatters, or leaks at normal operating pressure, stop the start-up, depressurise the equipment, and report the valve for bench testing. Start-up ends with the valve in service, its isolation proved open, and the discharge route clear.

## Normal operation

Keep the relief valve available at all times while the protected equipment is pressurised. Walk the line on each round and prove the valve as found. Confirm that the inlet and outlet block valves remain fully open and secured; a closed block valve removes the protection without any sign at the equipment itself. Listen for passing at the valve seat and feel the discharge line for a warmth that steady operation does not explain. Look for frost or condensate at the discharge outlet after any lift, and clear any obstruction at the outlet before the obstruction can freeze or plug. Keep the area around the valve clear for access at short notice. Never gag the valve, plug its outlet, or blank its inlet to stop a leak, and never adjust the set pressure at the line: set-pressure adjustment is a workshop task, carried out on the bench after removal. Record any simmering, leakage, or lift in the shift log with the equipment pressure at the time. Report a valve that lifts, leaks, or fails to reseat to the shift supervisor on the same shift. Normal operation asks little of the valve; the round exists to prove that nothing has taken its protection away.

## Alarms

The chapter recognises two alarms. Treat any other alarm on the protected equipment under the equipment chapter, and leave the relief valve as found unless an action below states otherwise.

High pressure in the protected equipment. Go to the relief valve and confirm that the valve is discharging: the discharge line warms and the valve is audible at the outlet. Watch the equipment pressure while the valve discharges. If the pressure falls, hold the equipment steady and let the valve reseat. If the pressure continues to rise with the valve discharging, shut off the source of pressure to the equipment: stop the feed, stop the heating input, and inform the shift supervisor at once. Stay at the equipment until the pressure is falling and the supervisor has taken the report.

Relief valve passing. The discharge line stays warm, or flow is audible at the valve, after the equipment pressure has returned to its normal level. Inform the shift supervisor and keep the equipment pressure under close watch. Raise a maintenance request for removal and bench testing of the valve. Do not isolate the valve while the equipment remains pressurised; the equipment keeps its protection until a planned changeover or a shutdown. Record each alarm and the action taken in the shift log before the shift ends. The two responses are distinct: prove the valve is working when the pressure is high, and report the valve when it passes at normal pressure.

## Shutdown

Take the relief valve out of service only after the protected equipment is depressurised. Reduce the equipment pressure to zero by the normal let-down route and prove the state at the gauge. Open the vent on the protected equipment and prove that no pressure remains before any line is broken. Close the inlet and outlet block valves and apply the isolation lock and tag. Drain the discharge line to its drain point, and leave the drain open while the valve is out of service. Hand the valve over for removal only when the isolation is proved and recorded; removal, overhaul, and bench testing belong to the maintenance procedure. On the return of the valve from the bench, restore the valve under the start-up section: check the nameplate against the test certificate, prove the block valves open and secured, and watch the first pressurisation. Shutdown leaves the equipment depressurised, the valve isolated and drained, and its return governed by the start-up checks.
